extracted.intended_audience: students and scholars of logic, philosophy of science, and foundations of mathematics
extracted.subtask_description: Identify and apply the criteria the author gives for sound inductive and deductive reasoning, for distinguishing experimental vs. deductive sciences, and for the admissibility of hypotheses and axioms (with geometric examples).

rubrics_metrics.name: Marks and chains of marks (a is a mark of b)
rubrics_metrics.description: Reasoning proceeds by recognizing 'marks' (observable circumstances) that indicate some property; several marks united at the extremity can together be a mark of another property (chains of marks). Example: rays of light + parabolic surface + parallelism are each a mark that jointly mark that reflected rays pass through the focus.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use observable or inferable 'marks' as the building blocks of inference; combine multiple marks where no single mark suffices. The example (parabolic reflector) shows how separate inductions may be combined to deduce a conclusion that no single induction would yield alone.

rubrics_metrics.name: Every step in ratiocination is an act of induction
rubrics_metrics.description: Even in deductive or demonstrative sciences, each step of reasoning (each inference in a train of deduction) is ultimately an induction from observed or assumed marks.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not treat deductions as free-standing from induction; when evaluating purportedly 'deductive' results, examine the underlying inductions and how cases are brought within their scope. Difficulty in mathematics often lies in recognizing that a particular case comes within the relevant inductions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Formulæ for inferring equality and inequality (the eight formulæ)
rubrics_metrics.description: For inferring equality: 'Things which being applied to each other coincide, are equals.'; 'Things which are equal to the same thing are equals.'; 'A whole and the sum of its parts are equals.'; 'The sums of equal things are equals.'; 'The differences of equal things are equals.' For inferring inequality: 'A whole and its parts are unequals.'; 'The sums of equal things and unequal things are unequals.'; 'The differences of equal things and unequal things are unequals.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These constitute the basic formulæ (marks) by which equality or inequality may be inferred. When proving that two things are equal or unequal, attempt to show that they possess one of these marks or can be brought within one of these formulæ by suitable constructions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Set of six constructive formulæ used to derive geometric propositions
rubrics_metrics.description: When reconstructing geometrical deductions from first principles one may rely on six formulæ: (1) 'The sums of equals are equal.' (2) 'Equal straight lines or angles, being applied to one another, coincide.' (3) 'Straight lines, having their extremities coincident, coincide.' (4) 'Angles, having their sides coincident, coincide.' (5) 'Things which coincide are equal.' (6) 'The differences of equals are equal.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use these as permissible inductive premises (marks) to demonstrate particular geometric truths (e.g., base angles of an isosceles triangle) without appealing to prior deductions; they show how to combine simple inductions to obtain more complex conclusions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Criterion for classifying a science as deductive or experimental (marks of marks)
rubrics_metrics.description: A science is deductive insofar as its propositions form chains a is a mark of b, b is a mark of c, c of d, ... allowing one to infer a is a mark of e (marks of marks). A science is experimental insofar as its generalizations remain detached and unconnected (no discovered marks-of-marks).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: To assess whether a domain is deductive, look for connecting inductions that permit chaining marks; absence of such links indicates the domain remains primarily experimental. Use this criterion when evaluating claims about a field's method.

rubrics_metrics.name: Transformation of experimental into deductive by discovering connecting inductions
rubrics_metrics.description: An experimental science can become deductive if new inductions are discovered that bridge previously unconnected generalizations (e.g., finding that b is a mark of c allows deducing a is a mark of c).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When judging progress in a field, reward discoveries that establish such connections (they reduce reliance on fresh experiments for each new case). Examples: Newton connecting planetary motions to centripetal force; possible future chemical connections (Liebig remark).

rubrics_metrics.name: Mathematics (science of number) as the chief agent of deductive extension
rubrics_metrics.description: Because properties of number apply universally (to quantity), discovering that qualitative variations correspond to quantitative relations allows application of mathematical theorems, making those qualitative theories more deductive.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate attempts to mathematize a domain by whether they establish reliable correspondences between quality and quantity. Successful mappings yield powerful deductive leverage (e.g., Descartes' analytic geometry, calculus applications).

rubrics_metrics.name: Prefer constructing sciences from the fewest and simplest inductions
rubrics_metrics.description: There are 'weighty scientific reasons' for giving each science as much deductive character as possible by building it from a small number of simple inductions and deriving complex cases by combining them.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When assessing theoretical frameworks, favor those that minimize primitive inductions and explain many phenomena by combinations of simple generalizations, provided corrections are applied where necessary.

rubrics_metrics.name: Admissibility requirement for hypotheses (must relate to real existence and not be distinctly false)
rubrics_metrics.description: Hypotheses framed to facilitate scientific inquiry must relate to something with real existence; they must not ascribe to objects any property which they do not possess (no distinctly false attributes). They may slightly exaggerate or suppress properties for convenience but must be corrected when those properties materially affect conclusions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Judge assumptions by whether they are realistic idealizations (small, restorable departures) rather than arbitrary fictions; require that suppressed properties be restored when they would make a material difference to result.

rubrics_metrics.name: Interpretation of 'necessary' and 'mathematical certainty' as conditional on hypotheses
rubrics_metrics.description: The necessity ascribed to mathematical truths is an illusion: such truths are necessary only in the sense that they follow correctly from the suppositions (definitions/axioms) adopted; those suppositions themselves are often hypotheses that depart from exact truth.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In evaluating claims of necessity or certainty, inspect the underlying hypotheses; treat mathematical certitude as conditional logical consequence rather than metaphysical necessity about real objects.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinction between axioms and definitions; some axioms are indemonstrable and true without hypothesis
rubrics_metrics.description: Definitions (first principles) in geometry are often hypotheses or idealizations, whereas axioms include some fundamental truths that are true without any mixture of hypothesis (e.g., 'Two straight lines which intersect each other cannot both be parallel to a third line' / Playfair-type property).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When analyzing foundations, separate what is an assumptive definition (approximation for convenience) from axioms claimed to be universally true; ensure indispensable axioms are not covertly treated as mere conveniences.

rubrics_metrics.name: Practical acceptability of idealizations in geometry and need for corrections when necessary
rubrics_metrics.description: Geometric definitions (points, lines, circles) do not exactly correspond to physical reality; we feign exactness for convenience. This is acceptable so long as the ignored irregularities do not materially affect results; where they do, conclusions must be corrected by adding propositions about aberrations or material properties.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate use of idealized models by whether the ignored deviations are negligible for the intended application; require explicit correction when physical properties (e.g., thickness, heat expansion) would appreciably alter conclusions.
